scenario_stem:
Fennel & Rye Bakery is a start-up opened 8 months ago by founder Dana Whitmore in the busy town of Millbrook, Country X. The bakery produces sourdough loaves and butter croissants for early commuters, employs 3 part-time assistants and recorded revenue of $3,400 last month against costs of $5,100, leaving a monthly loss of $1,700. Dana invested $9,000 of her savings and works around 55 hours a week.

The Country X government offers a start-up grant of $12,000 to new food businesses able to create at least 5 jobs, provided the owner matches it with $6,000 of her own capital and repays it if targets are missed. Alternatively, Millbrook Bank will lend Dana $15,000 at 9% interest over 4 years, or her flour supplier may allow 30 days of credit. Dana wants to open a second unit but lacks finance.

questions.question_text: Define 'grant'.
questions.model_answer: A grant is a sum of money given to a business by the government or another organisation that does not have to be repaid, usually to support a specific aim such as creating jobs. [2]

knowledge_max_2: A sum of money given to a business (usually by the government or an organisation)
Does not have to be repaid / given for a specific purpose such as job creation or supporting a start-up

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the Country X government offers grants to new businesses.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Grants encourage new businesses to create jobs, so unemployment falls and more people pay taxes [k]. The $12,000 grant requires at least 5 jobs, so the government expects direct employment benefits for Millbrook workers [app]. Reason 2: Supporting start-ups boosts competition and diversifies the local economy [k]. Dana must match the grant with $6,000 of her own capital, which shares the risk and reduces the cost to the government [app].

knowledge_max_2: Job creation / lower unemployment
Encourages enterprise, competition, economic growth or higher tax revenue
application_max_2: $12,000 grant tied to at least 5 jobs in Millbrook
Dana must match it with $6,000 of her own capital; renewed local food sector

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Fennel & Rye Bakery of accepting the government grant instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A grant does not have to be repaid, so Dana avoids interest charges [k]. The Millbrook Bank loan of $15,000 at 9% over 4 years would cost about $5,400 in interest, whereas the $12,000 grant is free if targets are met [app]. This frees cash for flour, wages and equipment during loss-making months, improving the bakery's chance of survival [an]. Benefit 2: Winning the grant gives the bakery credibility with suppliers and banks [k]. Dana is losing $1,700 every month and relies on 30 days of flour supplier credit, so government approval would reassure creditors that she can expand safely [app]. Stronger credibility may unlock better credit terms and wholesale accounts, helping revenue recover from $3,400 per month [an].

knowledge_max_2: Grant does not need to be repaid / no interest payable
Improves credibility and access to finance or suppliers
application_max_2: Bank loan $15,000 at 9% over 4 years (about $5,400 interest) vs free $12,000 grant
Monthly loss of $1,700 and reliance on 30 days supplier credit
analysis_max_2: Saves cash so fixed costs can be met, reducing risk of business failure
Credibility improves supplier terms, lifting revenue and supporting expansion

questions.question_text: Do you think Dana should accept the government grant? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Dana could accept the grant because it provides $12,000 with no interest, directly addressing her shortage of finance while she records a loss of $1,700 a month [k]. The money would fund a second unit and the 5-job target matches her expansion plan, and it avoids the $5,400 interest she would pay on the $15,000 bank loan [app]. Avoiding that interest directly reduces her outgoings and protects her working capital while she is loss-making [an]. However, the grant must be matched with $6,000 of her own matching capital and repaid if targets are missed, which is risky when revenue is only $3,400 a month [k]. Failing to create 5 jobs in time would force repayment and destroy her remaining cash, so poor planning or slow sales could make the bakery fail [an]. On the other hand, the bank loan gives full flexibility with no job conditions and a longer 4-year repayment structure [app]. Overall, Dana should accept the grant because it removes her biggest constraint, finance, and the target is realistic given the commuter demand for sourdough loaves, but only if she secures the 30 days of supplier credit first [eval]. She should track cash flow weekly and hire gradually so the 5 jobs are sustainable [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Grant gives finance with no interest / supports growth
Grant conditions (matching capital, repayment, job target) create risk
application_max_2: $12,000 grant vs $15,000 loan at 9% (about $5,400 interest); matching $6,000 plus existing $9,000 savings invested
Monthly loss $1,700, revenue $3,400, second unit plan, 5 jobs target
analysis_max_2: Removing interest cost preserves cash and improves survival odds
Missing job target triggers repayment, straining cash flow and risking failure
evaluation_max_2: Overall justified position weighing grant benefits against repayment risk
Recommendation tied to cash-flow monitoring / securing supplier credit before accepting

scenario_stem:
Brightbyte Apps is a software start-up founded 6 months ago by Lena Ortiz, a self-taught programmer who left her office job in the capital, Country X. Working from her spare bedroom, she is building an inventory app for small shops and charges 4 shop clients $700 each per month, giving revenue of $2,800 against monthly costs of $3,100. Her $14,000 savings are nearly exhausted and she has no written business plan.

Country X's New Enterprise Incubator offers start-ups 12 months of free desk space, weekly training in bookkeeping and marketing, weekly mentoring and a $10,000 grant, but requires relocation 40 km to the capital and the employment of at least 1 full-time developer. Lena could instead remain home-based with minimal overheads, though without training or support. She is unsure which option to choose.

questions.question_text: Define 'business plan'.
questions.model_answer: A business plan is a document that describes the business, its objectives, the market, forecasts and how the business will be financed and run, used to guide the owner and persuade lenders or investors. [2]

knowledge_max_2: A written document describing the business and its objectives/market/forecasts
Used to guide the business and to persuade financiers to lend or invest

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why many new businesses fail.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Many new businesses lack finance and run out of cash before they become profitable [k]. Lena's revenue of $2,800 is below her monthly costs of $3,100, so she burns through her $14,000 savings every month [app]. Reason 2: Poor planning causes failure because owners do not set objectives or forecast cash needs [k]. Lena has no written business plan, so nobody has tested whether 4 shop clients can ever cover her costs [app].

knowledge_max_2: Lack of finance / poor cash-flow management
Poor planning (no business plan or objectives)
application_max_2: Revenue $2,800 versus costs $3,100 per month
$14,000 savings nearly exhausted; no written business plan

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Lena may face if she rejects the incubator place.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Without the incubator's weekly training, Lena would lack bookkeeping and marketing skills, which are common causes of start-up failure [k]. She currently has no written business plan and mismanages money, so guessing instead of monitoring means she may not notice that $3,100 of monthly costs are unsustainable [app]. Poor financial control would likely force her to close within months [an]. Problem 2: Rejecting the incubator forfeits the $10,000 grant and free desk space, leaving her to fund everything herself [k]. Her $14,000 savings are nearly exhausted and she still owes money for software tools, so she cannot hire the full-time developer she needs to grow [app]. Without extra hands, app development slows, clients churn and revenue of $2,800 per month stagnates [an].

knowledge_max_2: Lack of training/skills leads to poor decisions and failure
Rejecting support forfeits grants and resources needed to grow
application_max_2: No written business plan; costs $3,100 exceed revenue $2,800
$14,000 savings nearly exhausted; incubator offers $10,000 grant and free desk space
analysis_max_2: Poor cash management accelerates insolvency and closure
Under-resourcing slows development, hurting competitiveness and growth

questions.question_text: Do you think Lena should accept the incubator place? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Lena could accept the incubator place because it offers 12 months of free desk space, weekly training and a $10,000 grant, which would fix her two biggest weaknesses: poor planning and lack of finance [k]. With her $14,000 savings nearly exhausted and costs of $3,100 exceeding revenue of $2,800 each month, the grant alone would extend her runway by many months [app]. That extra runway lets her fix the planning weakness before savings run dry, turning a struggling start-up into a sustainable one [an]. However, accepting means relocating 40 km to the capital and hiring at least 1 full-time developer, adding a salary she may not afford [k]. If 4 shop clients cannot grow, the extra wage pushes monthly costs up further and she may be forced to use the $10,000 to cover losses rather than development [an]. On the other hand, remaining home-based keeps overheads minimal and lets her keep control while she wins more clients [app]. Overall, Lena should accept the incubator place because the training would teach her to write a proper business plan and control cash, and the $10,000 grant plus mentoring outweigh the relocation cost, provided she can sign at least 2 new clients first [eval]. Without a written plan she risks becoming another failed start-up, so structured support is the smarter option [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Incubator offers training, mentoring, grants and free premises
Incubator conditions add costs and relocation risk
application_max_2: $10,000 grant, 12 months free desk space, 40 km relocation, 1 full-time developer
Revenue $2,800 vs costs $3,100; $14,000 savings nearly exhausted
analysis_max_2: Training improves planning and cash control, reducing failure risk
Added salary and relocation may strain cash if client growth is slow
evaluation_max_2: Overall justified recommendation weighing grant benefits against relocation costs
Evaluation linked to client growth / cash-flow evidence from the stem

scenario_stem:
Truegreen Cleaning Products is a manufacturing start-up founded 1 year ago by Marcus Oyelaran, producing eco-friendly sprays and detergents in a rented unit in Fenwick, Country X. It employs 5 production workers, sells to 60 local shops and recorded revenue of $96,000 last year against costs of $88,000, a profit of $8,000. The mixing machinery is ageing and bottling capacity limits growth.

Country X has designated an enterprise zone 55 km away offering 100% first-year capital allowances on new machinery and 5 years of zero business rates. To qualify, Truegreen must invest $30,000 in new bottling equipment within 12 months and create 4 additional jobs. Alternatively, Marcus could stay in Fenwick, keep renting at $640 per month, and retain his loyal workforce.

questions.question_text: Define 'entrepreneur'.
questions.model_answer: An entrepreneur is a person who takes the financial risk of starting and running a business, organising the factors of production and aiming to make a profit. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Person who starts/organises and runs a business
Takes financial risk in the hope of making a profit

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to a start-up of locating in an enterprise zone.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Enterprise zones reduce start-up costs through tax incentives such as capital allowances and lower rates [k]. Truegreen would pay zero business rates for 5 years and receive 100% capital allowances on new machinery, lowering its fixed costs [app]. Benefit 2: Enterprise zones are designed to attract investment, so infrastructure and support services are often better [k]. The 55 km zone expects Truegreen to invest $30,000 and create 4 jobs, so shared services and utilities are geared toward new manufacturers [app].

knowledge_max_2: Tax incentives reduce business costs (capital allowances / lower rates)
Infrastructure, support and labour availability attract new firms
application_max_2: 100% capital allowances and 5 years of zero business rates
Must invest $30,000 and create 4 jobs in the 55 km zone

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Truegreen may face if it relocates to the enterprise zone.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Relocation means the $30,000 investment in bottling equipment must be funded up front, increasing risk if sales disappoint [k]. Truegreen made only $8,000 profit on $96,000 revenue last year, so borrowing or using reserves for the new machinery could strain cash flow badly [app]. If 60 local shops do not expand with it, the business may fail while still owing for the equipment [an]. Problem 2: Moving 55 km away breaks links with the loyal fenwick workforce and existing local shop customers [k]. Staying means keeping staff and paying $640 per month rent, whereas relocation forces the creation of 4 additional jobs at unknown wages [app]. Lost local goodwill and higher labour costs could wipe out the saving from zero business rates, shrinking the thin $8,000 profit further [an].

knowledge_max_2: Large up-front capital investment increases financial risk
Relocation can disrupt staffing and existing customer relationships
application_max_2: Profit of $8,000 on revenue of $96,000 last year; $30,000 investment required within 12 months
Fenwick rent of $640 per month; 5 loyal production workers and 60 local shops
analysis_max_2: High fixed outgoings strain cash, increasing risk of insolvency
Lost goodwill/higher labour costs erode the tax saving, harming profitability

questions.question_text: Do you think Truegreen should relocate to the enterprise zone? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Truegreen could relocate because 100% capital allowances on new machinery and 5 years of zero business rates would cut its costs significantly, helping a business managing only $8,000 profit on $96,000 revenue [k]. Relocation also unlocks new bottling capacity, which currently limits growth, and the $30,000 incentive could be repaid quickly through higher sales [app]. Cutting fixed costs frees cash for materials and wages, compounding the benefit month after month [an]. However, the scheme demands a $30,000 investment within 12 months and 4 additional jobs, which may strain cash flow and force borrowing at bad terms [k]. If demand from the 60 local shops does not grow, the new machinery sits idle while wages and depreciation mount, pushing the firm towards failure [an]. On the other hand, staying in Fenwick keeps costs at $640 per month with a loyal workforce and familiar customers, but the ageing machinery keeps capacity capped and profits stuck at $8,000 [app]. Overall, Truegreen should relocate, but only after securing orders covering at least 70% of the new capacity and matching finance in place, because the tax incentives and bottling capacity are essential for growth while staying leaves it permanently capacity-constrained [eval]. If finance cannot be secured risk-free, staying is the safer short-term choice [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Enterprise zones offer tax incentives (capital allowances, zero rates) to attract firms
Relocation brings investment/job obligations and disruption risks
application_max_2: 100% capital allowances, 5 years zero business rates, $30,000 investment in 12 months, 4 additional jobs
Profit $8,000 on $96,000 revenue; 60 local shops; Fenwick rent $640 per month
analysis_max_2: Tax savings and new capacity raise profit potential and growth
Obligations strain cash; unused capacity and higher wages could erase benefits
evaluation_max_2: Overall justified recommendation weighing tax savings against relocation risk
Evaluation tied to securing orders/finance before the 12-month deadline

scenario_stem:
Aquajet Mobile Valeting is a start-up founded 2 years ago by Danny Herrera in Bracknell, Country X, offering van-based car washing and detailing to households across the town. It employs 2 part-time attendants and revenue fell from $9,800 per month to $6,300 per month over 6 months while costs stayed at $7,500 per month. Danny has missed 2 van loan payments and lost 1 supplier.

Country X's hardship scheme offers struggling start-ups a one-off $5,000 grant plus free budgeting training, but applicants must file a weekly cash-flow forecast for 6 consecutive months. Alternatively, Danny could ask his cleaning-supplies supplier for 45 days of credit and raise prices by 8%. He worries that poor planning, not demand, has caused his cash-flow crisis.

questions.question_text: Define 'cash-flow forecast'.
questions.model_answer: A cash-flow forecast is a plan estimating the likely cash inflows and outflows of a business over a future period, showing the expected bank balance. [2]

knowledge_max_2: A forecast/estimate of future cash inflows and outflows
Shows expected bank balance / helps plan for cash shortfalls

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why many new businesses experience cash-flow problems.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Many new businesses fail to plan their cash needs, so inflows arrive later than bills [k]. Danny's revenue fell to $6,300 while costs stayed at $7,500, a gap of $1,200 a month that he apparently did not forecast [app]. Reason 2: Over-reliance on credit sales and suppliers can leave firms short of cash [k]. Danny missed 2 van loan payments and lost a supplier, showing his outflows are being called in faster than his inflows arrive [app].

knowledge_max_2: Poor planning / no cash-flow forecast
Timing mismatch between inflows and outflows / reliance on credit
application_max_2: Revenue $6,300 per month vs costs $7,500 per month (a $1,200 monthly gap)
2 missed van loan payments and a lost supplier

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Aquajet Mobile Valeting of producing a weekly cash-flow forecast.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A weekly forecast shows Danny exactly when cash shortages will occur so he can act before bills go unpaid [k]. His costs of $7,500 exceed the $6,300 of revenue by $1,200 per month, so a forecast would expose the gap early enough to arrange credit or cut spending [app]. Acting early avoids more missed van loan payments and protects the business from collapse [an]. Benefit 2: The forecast is a required input for the hardship scheme, unlocking the $5,000 grant and free budgeting training [k]. Filing it for 6 consecutive months is mandatory, and the grant plus training would directly tackle his poor planning [app]. Better budgeting skills would stop the decline in revenue from $9,800 to $6,300 going unnoticed, restoring control over cash [an].

knowledge_max_2: Identifies shortages early / enables corrective action
Satisfies grant requirements and builds financial control
application_max_2: Costs $7,500 exceed revenue $6,300 by $1,200 per month; missed 2 van loan payments
Hardship scheme requires weekly forecast for 6 months; grant is $5,000
analysis_max_2: Early action prevents insolvency and protects the business
Better financial control slows/reverses the revenue decline, improving viability

questions.question_text: Do you think Danny should accept the hardship grant? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Danny could accept the hardship grant because the $5,000 one-off payment would cover more than 4 months of his $1,200 monthly cash gap and the free budgeting training targets his weak planning directly [k]. His revenue has fallen from $9,800 to $6,300 while costs stayed at $7,500, so cash support plus skills would address the root cause rather than the symptoms [app]. Fixing the planning weakness now tackles the real cause of failure instead of masking it [an]. However, the scheme demands a weekly cash-flow forecast for 6 consecutive months, plus follow-up checks, which adds administrative work while he is struggling to survive [k]. If he stops filing or forecasts poorly, the grant could be withdrawn and he gains nothing except extra pressure [an]. On the other hand, simply raising prices by 8% and asking for 45 days of credit would improve cash without conditions, though it may drive away price-sensitive households [app]. Overall, Danny should accept the hardship grant because it fixes both the finance and planning problems together, whereas credit terms merely delay the cash gap; the forecasting discipline he builds is exactly what a failing start-up needs [eval]. He should also raise prices gradually and confirm the credit deal in writing alongside the grant [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Grant provides emergency finance and training support
Grant conditions (weekly forecasts, compliance) impose burdens
application_max_2: $5,000 grant; revenue down from $9,800 to $6,300 vs costs of $7,500 (gap $1,200/month)
Alternative: 45 days credit and 8% price rise; 2 missed van loan payments
analysis_max_2: Grant plus training addresses root cause (poor planning), improving survival
Conditions add burden; failure to comply risks losing the grant
evaluation_max_2: Overall justified position weighing grant support against conditions
Evaluation tied to combining grant with price rise/credit and monitoring

scenario_stem:
Hillcrest Alpaca Experiences is a rural start-up founded 10 months ago by Anna and Ben Kovac on their farm near Marlow, Country X. Visitors pay $25 each to walk and feed the 5 alpacas; in the first 6 months the farm hosted an average of 120 visitors per month, earning $18,000. Monthly costs are $1,900 and the couple want to buy 3 more alpacas at $2,400 each.

Country X's Rural Enterprise Scheme offers grants of up to $8,000 plus 20 hours of free training in marketing and bookkeeping to rural businesses creating at least 2 jobs, but applicants must submit a written business plan by 31 March and match 30% of the grant. The Kovacs could instead self-fund the $7,200 expansion from their savings and keep full control.

questions.question_text: Define 'opportunity cost'.
questions.model_answer: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative foregone when a choice is made. [2]

knowledge_max_2: The value of the next best alternative given up
Incurred whenever a choice is made because resources are scarce

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the government supports businesses in rural areas.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Rural areas often suffer high unemployment and low incomes, so government support spreads economic activity [k]. The Rural Enterprise Scheme targets rural businesses like the Kovacs' farm, aiming to create at least 2 jobs in the Marlow area [app]. Reason 2: Supporting rural start-ups slows migration to cities and protects communities [k]. The scheme offers up to $8,000 plus 20 hours of free training, encouraging new rural ventures that keep residents and visitors spending locally [app].

knowledge_max_2: Reduce rural unemployment / raise rural incomes
Encourage balanced regional development / stem urban migration
application_max_2: Rural Enterprise Scheme grant up to $8,000 tied to at least 2 jobs near Marlow
Farm near Marlow; 20 hours of free training to rural businesses

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the Rural Enterprise Scheme for Hillcrest Alpaca Experiences.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: The grant of up to $8,000 would fund most of the $7,200 alpaca expansion without draining the couple's savings [k]. Self-funding would swallow their entire cushion, but the scheme requires only a 30% match, so they keep reserves for emergencies [app]. Retained savings protect the business if visitor numbers fall in winter, improving survival odds [an]. Benefit 2: The 20 hours of free training in marketing and bookkeeping would build skills the couple lacks [k]. Many rural start-ups fail through poor record-keeping and weak promotion, and the Kovacs currently track bookings informally across 120 visitors a month [app]. Better records and marketing would let them price, plan and promote professionally, increasing visitor numbers and revenue beyond the current $18,000 [an].

knowledge_max_2: Grant funding reduces the owner's own financial outlay / preserves reserves
Free training improves skills (marketing, bookkeeping)
application_max_2: Grant up to $8,000 covers the $7,200 expansion; only 30% matching required
Visitors pay $25 each; average 120 visitors per month; revenue $18,000 so far
analysis_max_2: Preserving savings increases resilience and survival chances
Improved skills raise visitor numbers, revenue and long-term growth

questions.question_text: Do you think Anna and Ben should apply for the Rural Enterprise Scheme grant? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The Kovacs could apply because the scheme offers up to $8,000, more than the full $7,200 expansion, plus 20 hours of free marketing and bookkeeping training [k]. With a 30% match, applying would cost them about $2,400 of savings instead of $7,200, and it builds the skills needed to manage 120 visitors a month professionally [app]. Better skills plus preserved savings directly raise the odds of surviving the critical first years [an]. However, they must submit a written business plan by 31 March and create at least 2 jobs, conditions that take time and carry obligations [k]. If they fail to deliver or miss the deadline, they receive nothing and have lost valuable planning time during their peak visitor season [an]. On the other hand, self-funding keeps full control with no paperwork or job commitments, though it consumes nearly all their savings and leaves no buffer if winter bookings fall [app]. Overall, the Kovacs should apply, because the $4,800 saving ($7,200 minus the $2,400 match) and free training outweigh the effort, provided they can write a realistic business plan and commit to the 2 jobs [eval]. If the plan deadline slips or visitor demand proves seasonal, self-funding remains the fallback [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Grant reduces owner outlay and adds training (Rural Enterprise Scheme)
Grant has conditions: written plan, match, job creation
application_max_2: Grant up to $8,000 vs $7,200 expansion; 30% match (about $2,400); deadline 31 March
Average 120 visitors per month at $25; revenue $18,000; 20 hours training; 2 jobs required
analysis_max_2: Grant preserves savings, strengthening financial resilience
Conditions risk wasted effort/loss of control if demand is seasonal or plan fails
evaluation_max_2: Overall justified recommendation weighing grant benefits against conditions
Evaluation tied to business-plan feasibility / seasonal demand evidence in stem

scenario_stem:
Nettle & Thread Tailors is a start-up founded 1 year ago by Imogen Hartley, making made-to-measure suits and dresses in her converted garage in Wexley, Country X. She employs 1 part-time sewer and recorded revenue of $27,000 last year against costs of $31,000, a loss of $4,000. She has no written business plan, ran short of cash in month 4 and missed a $2,000 rent payment.

Country X's Start Smart programme offers 8 weeks of free evening sessions covering business plans, cash-flow forecasting and pricing, plus free mentoring for new entrepreneurs. Sessions run every Tuesday and Thursday, costing Imogen about $600 a month in lost paid work. Alternatively, she could pay a consultant $900 for a business plan prepared within 10 days.

questions.question_text: Define 'working capital'.
questions.model_answer: Working capital is the finance available to a business for its day-to-day operations, calculated as current assets minus current liabilities. [2]

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why writing a business plan is important for a start-up.

Imogen has no written business plan, and she ran short of cash in month 4 and missed a $2,000 rent payment [app]. Reason 2: A plan helps persuade banks and grant bodies to provide finance [k]. Country X's Start Smart scheme expects new entrepreneurs to produce plans, so Imogen's missing plan may block her access to grants and loans [app].

knowledge_max_2: Sets objectives/forecasts and reduces risk of failure
Needed to raise finance from banks or grant providers
application_max_2: Imogen has no written business plan; month 4 cash shortfall and $2,000 rent missed

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Nettle & Thread may face without a written business plan.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Without a plan she cannot forecast cash needs, so shortages arrive unannounced [k]. Her $27,000 revenue against $31,000 costs produced a $4,000 loss, and she still had to find $2,000 rent in month 4 with no savings buffer [app]. Unplanned outflows like that force missed payments and can push a sole trader out of business [an]. Problem 2: Without a plan she has no clear growth strategy or pricing, so growth stalls [k]. She is paying $600 a month in lost work while considering training, and a consultant would charge $900 for a plan she could not afford blindly [app]. Weak pricing and no targets mean the loss repeats next year instead of turning into profit [an].

Overall, Imogen should attend Start Smart, because the skills transfer — planning, forecasting and pricing — permanently fixes the cause of failure for the cost of $1,200 in lost work, beating a $900 consultant plan she cannot maintain [eval]. scenario_stem:
Solder & Spark Repairs is a start-up founded 14 months ago by Rafiq Chowdhury, repairing smartphones and tablets in a high-street unit in Redford, Country X. It employs 1 part-time technician and takes in $5,600 a month, while rent is $950 a month. Walk-by trade from the busy street generates about $2,000 of that monthly revenue.

Redford Council's enterprise centre offers start-ups low-cost premises at $480 per month for 2 years plus business rates relief, but the unit is 6 km away with no shopfront and half the floor space. Rafiq could renew the high-street lease at $950 per month and keep his passing trade, or move to the cheaper unit. He must decide before the lease expires on 30 September.

questions.question_text: Define 'tax incentive'.
questions.model_answer: A tax incentive is a reduction in, or relief from, tax offered by the government to encourage businesses to do something, for example investing or creating jobs. [2]

knowledge_max_2: A tax reduction/relief offered by the government
Designed to encourage business behaviour such as investing or hiring

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of low-cost premises for a start-up.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Low-cost premises cut fixed costs, leaving more cash for stock and wages [k].
